introduction_markdown: Multiple choice paper (0765 Pure Maths With Mechanics 1, June 2025, Advanced Level, one and a half hours). Answer ALL questions; each question has FOUR suggested answers A, B, C and D and only one answer must be marked (if more than one answer is marked the score for that question is zero). Formulae booklets and calculators are allowed. Section A: Pure Mathematics (questions 1 to 35); Section B: Mechanics (questions 36 to 50). Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room.

figures.legende: Figure 1 (Q46): particles P (weight 10 N) and Q (weight 40 N, labelled O on the scan) hanging from a light inextensible string over a fixed smooth pulley; tension T on each side.

incertitudes: Le sujet est un scan sans couche texte (6 pages : page de garde non numérotée puis pages 2 à 6), lu page par page en image, avec recadrages à 200 dpi (filigranes gcerevision.com ignorés). La page de garde indique bien « ADVANCED LEVEL », « 0765 Pure Maths With Mechanics 1 », juin 2025 ; 50 questions, aucune page manquante.

Questions 46 et 47 : leurs numéros ne sont pas visibles sur le scan (marge gauche rognée en haut de la page 6). Ils sont déduits de la suite 45 puis 48 : Q46 = schéma des particules P et Q, Q47 = trois particules de poids 7 N, 9 N, 4 N.

Question 46 : les poids (10 N pour P, 40 N pour Q) ne sont donnés que par le schéma, recadré dans la figure 1 ; la deuxième particule est étiquetée « O » sur le schéma alors que l'énoncé parle de Q : lu comme Q. g = 10 m/s2 est imposé par l'énoncé et utilisé tel quel.

Question 49 : le bord droit du scan est coupé : la première ligne (« A car moving at 5 m/s is brought to rest after ») est partiellement tronquée (« brough... rest after ») et le début de « The acceleration of the car is » aussi (« Th acceleration »). Texte reconstitué sans ambiguïté ; les données 5 m/s et 1,5 km sont parfaitement lisibles.
Question 1 : l'énoncé écrit f : R vers R alors que f n'est pas définie en x = -1 ; le domaine n'intervient pas dans la question, qui porte sur l'image (R privé de 1, option A).
Question 2 : l'énoncé dit « f(x) = 3x - 2 » alors que la fonction composée est g ; lu comme g(x) = 3x - 2 (seule lecture possible). (g o h)(x) = 3x - 5, option C.
Question 12 : l'option D est imprimée « Not reflecxive » (faute de frappe) ; transcrite « Not reflexive ». Seule l'option C (transitive) est vraie.
Question 31 : « can be form » (faute du sujet) conservé tel quel. La condition « au moins un garçon et une fille » exclut le cas (0 garçon, 5 filles) ; on trouve 45 (option A).
Question 37 : l'énoncé parle d'un « truck » puis du « car » (même véhicule) ; lu comme un seul véhicule de 1800 kg. Aucune valeur de g n'est nécessaire (route horizontale).

Question 44 : le sujet demande la vitesse scalaire (speed) ; l'option A est la vitesse relative vectorielle (-12i + 5j), non une vitesse scalaire ; seule la valeur 13 m/s (option C) est une vitesse scalaire correcte.

Question 41 : sphères lisses, choc direct : la quantité de mouvement se conserve le long de la ligne des centres ; vitesse finale de A = 1,5 m/s dans le sens initial de B (coefficient de restitution 0,25, compatible).
Constantes : aucune autre valeur de g n'est utilisée que celle de la question 46 (10 m/s2, imprimée).

Converties en questions ouvertes par le relecteur (clé ou options discutables) : 5, 10, 18, 19. Q5 : les options A et D sont toutes deux des vecteurs normaux (A = -D), clé attendue D. Q10 : l'équation imprimée 3^(2x) - 10(3^(x+1)) + 9 = 0 donne x = log base 3 de (15 +/- 6 racine de 6), soit environ 3,087 et -1,087, valeurs absentes des options ; la réponse visée D (x = 0 et x = 2) correspond à l'équation 3^(2x) - 10(3^x) + 9 = 0, exposant x probablement mal imprimé (x+1). Q18 : les options A et D sont imprimées identiquement (1 - 3x + 9x^2), toutes deux exactes. Q19 : la base du logarithme n'est pas imprimée ; en base 10 la solution est x = 0, absente des options ; l'option D (x = -2) n'est correcte qu'en base 2 (réponse visée D, hypothèse non confirmée).

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION A: PURE MATHEMATICS**

Given that $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, where $f(x)=\dfrac{x+2}{x+1}$, the range of $f$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Write $f(x)=\dfrac{x+2}{x+1}=1+\dfrac{1}{x+1}$. The term $\dfrac1{x+1}$ takes every real value except $0$ (it is never zero), so $f(x)$ takes every real value except $1$.

Algebraic check: put $y=\dfrac{x+2}{x+1}$. Then $y(x+1)=x+2$, so $x(y-1)=2-y$ and $x=\dfrac{2-y}{y-1}$, which exists exactly when $y\neq1$. The value $y=1$ would need $x+2=x+1$, which is impossible. Hence the range is $\{y\in\mathbb R:\ y\neq1\}$.

Option C, $x\neq-1$, describes the excluded value of the domain (where the denominator vanishes), not the range; B and D are not related to the function.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If functions $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ and function $h:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ are such that $f(x)=3x-2$ and $h(x)=x-1$, then $(g\circ h)(x)=$
questions.corrige_markdown:
The statement defines the rule $3x-2$ with the letter $f$ although the function being composed is called $g$; the only possible reading is $g(x)=3x-2$.

$(g\circ h)(x)=g(h(x))$: apply $h$ first, then $g$. So $(g\circ h)(x)=g(x-1)=3(x-1)-2=3x-3-2=3x-5$.

Option B is $(h\circ g)(x)=h(3x-2)=3x-3$, the composition in the wrong order. A and D come from sign slips when removing the brackets.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $\mathbf A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\4&5&6\\7&8&9\end{pmatrix}$, then the cofactor of the element $6$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The cofactor of the element $a_{ij}$ is $C_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}M_{ij}$, where the minor $M_{ij}$ is the determinant left when row $i$ and column $j$ are deleted.

The element $6$ is in row $2$, column $3$. Deleting row 2 and column 3 leaves $\begin{vmatrix}1&2\\7&8\end{vmatrix}$, so $M_{23}=1\cdot8-2\cdot7=-6$. The sign factor is $(-1)^{2+3}=-1$. Hence
$C_{23}=-\begin{vmatrix}1&2\\7&8\end{vmatrix}=-(-6)=6$.

Option A leaves out the sign; options C and D multiply by the element $6$ itself, which is part of a cofactor expansion ($a_{ij}C_{ij}$) but not of the cofactor.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $\dfrac{2x+1}{(1-x)(2+x)}\equiv\dfrac{A}{1-x}+\dfrac{B}{2+x}$, then
questions.corrige_markdown:
Multiply both sides by $(1-x)(2+x)$: $2x+1\equiv A(2+x)+B(1-x)$.

Put $x=1$: $3=3A$, so $A=1$. Put $x=-2$: $-3=3B$, so $B=-1$.

Check: $(2+x)-(1-x)=2x+1$. The other options come from sign errors when substituting the roots.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The normal vector to the plane $6x+2y-7z-12=0$ is

*Options as printed:* A) $-6\mathbf i-2\mathbf j+7\mathbf k$   B) $6\mathbf i+2\mathbf j-12\mathbf k$   C) $6\mathbf i-2\mathbf j-12\mathbf k$   D) $6\mathbf i+2\mathbf j-7\mathbf k$
questions.corrige_markdown:
For a plane $ax+by+cz=d$ the vector $a\mathbf i+b\mathbf j+c\mathbf k$ is perpendicular to the plane. Here $a=6$, $b=2$, $c=-7$, so the normal read from the coefficients is $6\mathbf i+2\mathbf j-7\mathbf k$ (option D).

Option A is the opposite vector $-(6\mathbf i+2\mathbf j-7\mathbf k)$: it is also perpendicular to the plane (any non-zero multiple of a normal is a normal), so strictly two options, A and D, are normal vectors. This is why the question is left open: the expected answer is D, but A cannot be called wrong. Options B and C include the constant term $-12$ as a component, which is a common error.

**Intended answer: D ($6\mathbf i+2\mathbf j-7\mathbf k$).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are roots of a quadratic equation such that $\alpha+\beta=3$ and $\alpha\beta=\dfrac32$. The value of $\alpha^2+\beta^2=$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Use $\alpha^2+\beta^2=(\alpha+\beta)^2-2\alpha\beta=3^2-2\cdot\dfrac32=9-3=6$.

Option D forgets to subtract $2\alpha\beta$; option A adds $2\alpha\beta$ instead of subtracting it.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: When $f(x)=2x^3+x^2-13x+6$ is divided by $x+1$ the remainder is
questions.corrige_markdown:
By the remainder theorem, the remainder on division by $x+1=x-(-1)$ is $f(-1)$:
$f(-1)=2(-1)^3+(-1)^2-13(-1)+6=-2+1+13+6=18$.

Option B, $-4$, is $f(1)$ (the remainder on division by $x-1$); options A and D are not values of $f$ at $x=-1$.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The range of values of $x$ for which $|x+4|\le2$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
$|x+4|\le2$ means $-2\le x+4\le2$. Subtracting $4$ throughout gives $-6\le x\le-2$.

Option B is the solution set of the opposite inequality $|x+4|\ge2$ (a distance greater than or equal to $2$ from $-4$); A and C are only halves of it.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $\sin\theta=\dfrac45$ and $\theta$ is an acute angle, then the exact value of $2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Since $\theta$ is acute, $\cos\theta>0$ and $\cos\theta=\sqrt{1-\sin^2\theta}=\sqrt{1-\dfrac{16}{25}}=\dfrac35$.

Then $2\sin\theta\cos\theta=\sin2\theta=2\cdot\dfrac45\cdot\dfrac35=\dfrac{24}{25}$.

Traps: $\dfrac{16}{25}=\sin^2\theta$, $\dfrac9{25}=\cos^2\theta$, and $\dfrac{12}{25}=\sin\theta\cos\theta$ (the factor $2$ forgotten).

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The values of $x$ that satisfy the equation $3^{2x}-10\left(3^{x+1}\right)+9=0$ are

*Options as printed:* A) $x=1,\ x=9$   B) $x=-2,\ x=0$   C) $x=-1,\ x=-9$   D) $x=0,\ x=2$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $u=3^x>0$, so that $3^{2x}=u^2$ and $3^{x+1}=3u$.

**As printed**, $3^{2x}-10\left(3^{x+1}\right)+9=0$ becomes $u^2-30u+9=0$, so $u=15\pm6\sqrt6$ (both positive) and $x=\log_3\left(15\pm6\sqrt6\right)\approx3.087$ or $-1.087$. None of these values is in the list of options (substituting $x=1,9,-2,0,-1,-9,2$ never gives $0$).

**Probable intended equation**: $3^{2x}-10\left(3^{x}\right)+9=0$ (exponent $x$, not $x+1$). Then $u^2-10u+9=0$, so $(u-1)(u-9)=0$, $u=1$ or $u=9$, hence $3^x=1$ gives $x=0$ and $3^x=9$ gives $x=2$. Check: $x=0$: $1-10+9=0$; $x=2$: $81-90+9=0$. This is option D.

The printed exponent and the options are inconsistent, which is why the question is left open: the intended answer is D only under the corrected equation.

**Intended answer: D ($x=0,\ x=2$).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: If $y=0$ when $x=2$, then the solution of the differential equation $y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Separate the variables: $\displaystyle\int y\,dy=\int x\,dx$, so $\dfrac{y^2}{2}=\dfrac{x^2}{2}+C$, that is $y^2=x^2+K$ with $K=2C$.

Use $y=0$ when $x=2$: $0=4+K$, so $K=-4$ and $y^2=x^2-4$.

Check: differentiating gives $2y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2x$, i.e. $y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x$, and $x=2$ gives $y^2=0$. Options A, C and D use a wrong constant.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: On the set $A=\{2,4,8,16\}$, a relation $R$ is defined by $x\,R\,y$ if and only if $y$ is a multiple of $x$. $R$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Test the three properties on $A=\{2,4,8,16\}$.

- Reflexive: every $x$ is a multiple of itself ($x=1\cdot x$), so $xRx$ for all $x$. R is reflexive, which rules out D.
- Symmetric: $2R4$ holds ($4=2\cdot2$) but $4R2$ does not ($2$ is not a multiple of $4$). R is not symmetric, which rules out B (and A, because an equivalence relation must be symmetric).
- Transitive: if $y=kx$ and $z=my$ with $k,m$ integers, then $z=(mk)x$ is a multiple of $x$, so $xRy$ and $yRz$ give $xRz$. R is transitive.

R is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive (a partial order), so the only true statement is that R is transitive.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The line segment $AB$, where $A(5,5)$ and $B(3,-2)$, is the diameter of a circle. The equation of the circle is
questions.corrige_markdown:
A point $P(x,y)$ lies on the circle with diameter $AB$ exactly when $\overrightarrow{PA}\cdot\overrightarrow{PB}=0$ (angle in a semicircle). With $A(x_1,y_1)$ and $B(x_2,y_2)$ this gives
$(x-x_1)(x-x_2)+(y-y_1)(y-y_2)=0$.

Here $x_1=5$, $y_1=5$, $x_2=3$, $y_2=-2$: $(x-5)(x-3)+(y-5)(y+2)=0$. Expanded: $x^2+y^2-8x-3y+5=0$, centre $\left(4,\tfrac32\right)$, the midpoint of $AB$, and $r^2=\dfrac{AB^2}{4}=\dfrac{4+49}{4}=\dfrac{53}{4}$, which agrees.

Options A, B and C each contain a sign error in one of the factors ($y-2$ instead of $y+2$, $x+3$ instead of $x-3$, $y+5$ instead of $y-5$).

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Two vectors $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ are given as $\mathbf a=\mathbf i+3\mathbf j+2\mathbf k$ and $\mathbf b=2\mathbf i-\mathbf j+2\mathbf k$. The vector product $\mathbf a\times\mathbf b$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
$\mathbf a\times\mathbf b=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\1&3&2\\2&-1&2\end{vmatrix}
=\mathbf i(3\cdot2-2\cdot(-1))-\mathbf j(1\cdot2-2\cdot2)+\mathbf k(1\cdot(-1)-3\cdot2)$
$=8\mathbf i+2\mathbf j-7\mathbf k$.

Check: the result must be perpendicular to both vectors: $\mathbf a\cdot(8,2,-7)=8+6-14=0$ and $\mathbf b\cdot(8,2,-7)=16-2-14=0$. Options B, C and D make a sign slip in the $\mathbf j$ or $\mathbf k$ component.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The volume generated when the area of the finite region enclosed by the $x$-axis and the curve $y=2x^2-4x$ is rotated completely about the $x$-axis is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The curve $y=2x^2-4x=2x(x-2)$ meets the $x$-axis at $x=0$ and $x=2$; the finite region lies between these values. Rotating about the $x$-axis, the volume is $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_a^b y^2\,dx$ with $a=0$, $b=2$:
$V=\pi\displaystyle\int_0^2(2x^2-4x)^2\,dx$.

(Value: $\pi\displaystyle\int_0^2(4x^4-16x^3+16x^2)\,dx=\pi\left(\dfrac{128}{5}-64+\dfrac{128}{3}\right)=\dfrac{64\pi}{15}$.)

Options A, C and D use the wrong interval ($-2$ is not a root) and, for C and D, a factor $2\pi$, which is not the formula for rotation about the $x$-axis.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A root of the equation $x^3+x-26=0$ lies between
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $f(x)=x^3+x-26$, continuous for all $x$. Then $f(1)=-24$, $f(2)=8+2-26=-16$, $f(3)=27+3-26=4$, $f(4)=42$, $f(5)=104$.

$f(2)<0<f(3)$: the sign changes between $2$ and $3$, so by the intermediate value theorem a root lies in $(2,3)$. In the other intervals $f$ has the same sign at both ends, so no sign change is detected.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The sum of the first $n$ terms of a sequence is given by $S_n=2n^2+n$. The $n^{\text{th}}$ term of this sequence is
questions.corrige_markdown:
For $n\ge2$, $u_n=S_n-S_{n-1}=(2n^2+n)-\left[2(n-1)^2+(n-1)\right]=2n^2+n-2n^2+4n-2-n+1=4n-1$.

For $n=1$: $u_1=S_1=3=4(1)-1$, so the formula also holds for $n=1$. The sequence $3,7,11,\dots$ is arithmetic with common difference $4$.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The first three terms in the binomial expansion of $(1+3x)^{-1}$ are

*Options as printed:* A) $1-3x+9x^2$   B) $1+3x-9x^2$   C) $1-3x-9x^2$   D) $1-3x+9x^2$
questions.corrige_markdown:
For $|x|<\tfrac13$: $(1+3x)^{-1}=1+(-1)(3x)+\dfrac{(-1)(-2)}{2!}(3x)^2+\cdots=1-3x+9x^2-\cdots$.

Check with the geometric series $\dfrac1{1+r}=1-r+r^2-\cdots$ where $r=3x$. So the correct expansion is $1-3x+9x^2$. Options B and C have wrong signs.

Defect of the printed question: options A and D are printed identically ($1-3x+9x^2$), so two options are correct at once. The question is therefore left open.

**Answer: A (and D, which is identical).**

**Intended answer: A ($1-3x+9x^2$).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The value of $x$ for which $\log2+\log(2x+5)=1$ is

*Options as printed:* A) $2$   B) $-\dfrac12$   C) $\dfrac12$   D) $-2$
questions.corrige_markdown:
**With common logarithms (base 10)**, as the notation $\log$ normally means: $\log2+\log(2x+5)=\log\left[2(2x+5)\right]=1$ gives $2(2x+5)=10$, so $2x+5=5$ and $x=0$. The condition $2x+5>0$ holds. The value $x=0$ is not among the options. (With natural logarithms the equation gives $x=\dfrac{e-10}{4}\approx-1.82$, not an option either.)

**With logarithms to base 2** (where $\log_22=1$): $\log_22+\log_2(2x+5)=1$ gives $\log_2(2x+5)=0$, so $2x+5=1$ and $x=-2$. Check: $\log_22+\log_21=1+0=1$. This is option D, the only option for which the equation holds in some standard reading.

The base of the logarithm is not printed, and the base-10 reading has no correct option, so the question cannot be marked automatically: it is left open. The most likely intended answer is D (base 2).

**Intended answer: D ($-2$).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to2}\left(\dfrac{x-2}{x^2-5x+6}\right)=$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Direct substitution gives $\dfrac00$, so factorise: $x^2-5x+6=(x-2)(x-3)$. For $x\neq2$ the fraction equals $\dfrac1{x-3}$. Hence
$\displaystyle\lim_{x\to2}\dfrac{x-2}{(x-2)(x-3)}=\lim_{x\to2}\dfrac1{x-3}=\dfrac1{2-3}=-1$.

Option D, $1$, comes from $\dfrac1{3-2}$ (sign slip).

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\int_0^1\dfrac{x}{1+x^2}\,dx=$
questions.corrige_markdown:
The numerator is half the derivative of the denominator: $\dfrac{d}{dx}(1+x^2)=2x$. So
$\displaystyle\int_0^1\dfrac{x}{1+x^2}\,dx=\left[\dfrac12\ln(1+x^2)\right]_0^1=\dfrac12\ln2-\dfrac12\ln1=\dfrac12\ln2\approx0.3466$.

Option A forgets the factor $\dfrac12$; option D, $\dfrac12\ln4=\ln2$, has the same value as A and is also wrong; B is $2\ln2$.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $y^3=12x-x^3$ then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$ (chain rule on $y^3$): $3y^2\dfrac{dy}{dx}=12-3x^2$, so
$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{12-3x^2}{3y^2}=\dfrac{4-x^2}{y^2}$.

Option A has the opposite sign; B and C lose the minus sign of $-x^3$ on differentiation.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The complex number $z=\dfrac{1+2i}{3-4i}$ can be expressed in the form $a+bi$ as
questions.corrige_markdown:
Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate $3+4i$ of the denominator:
$z=\dfrac{(1+2i)(3+4i)}{(3-4i)(3+4i)}=\dfrac{3+4i+6i+8i^2}{9+16}=\dfrac{-5+10i}{25}=-\dfrac15+\dfrac25i$.

Check: $\left(-\dfrac15+\dfrac25i\right)(3-4i)=-\dfrac35+\dfrac45i+\dfrac65i+\dfrac85=1+2i$.

Option A comes from using $i^2=+1$ (the real part becomes $3+8=11$); B and C come from further sign errors.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The argument of the complex number $z=\dfrac{1+i\sqrt3}{1+i}$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
$\arg(1+i\sqrt3)=\dfrac\pi3$ (modulus $2$) and $\arg(1+i)=\dfrac\pi4$ (modulus $\sqrt2$). For a quotient, $\arg\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}=\arg z_1-\arg z_2$, so
$\arg z=\dfrac\pi3-\dfrac\pi4=\dfrac{\pi}{12}$.

Check: $|z|=\sqrt2$ and $z=\dfrac{(1+i\sqrt3)(1-i)}{2}=\dfrac{(1+\sqrt3)+i(\sqrt3-1)}{2}$, which lies in the first quadrant and has $\tan(\arg z)=\dfrac{\sqrt3-1}{\sqrt3+1}=2-\sqrt3=\tan15^\circ$. Option C is the sum $\dfrac\pi3+\dfrac\pi4$ (wrong rule); D is the negative of the correct value.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The general solution of the equation $\sin\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The principal value is $\alpha=\dfrac\pi3$ because $\sin\dfrac\pi3=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$. The general solution of $\sin\theta=\sin\alpha$ is $\theta=n\pi+(-1)^n\alpha$, $n\in\mathbb Z$, so $\theta=n\pi+(-1)^n\dfrac\pi3$.

Check: $n=0$ gives $\dfrac\pi3$; $n=1$ gives $\pi-\dfrac\pi3=\dfrac{2\pi}3$; both have sine $\dfrac{\sqrt3}2$. Options A and D (minus sign) give $-\dfrac\pi3$ for $n=0$, whose sine is negative; options B and D use $\dfrac\pi6$, the angle for $\sin\theta=\dfrac12$.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The tangent of the acute angle between the lines $y=5x-7$ and $y=x-6$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The gradients are $m_1=5$ and $m_2=1$. For the acute angle $\varphi$ between the lines,
$\tan\varphi=\left|\dfrac{m_1-m_2}{1+m_1m_2}\right|=\left|\dfrac{5-1}{1+5}\right|=\dfrac46=\dfrac23$.

The tangent of an acute angle is positive, so options B, C and D (negative) are impossible; $-\dfrac23$ would be the tangent of the obtuse angle.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The values of $y$ for various values of $x$ are given in the table below.

| $x$ | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $y$ | 2 | 3.2 | 4.2 | 5 | 5.7 | 6.3 |

Using the trapezium rule, $\displaystyle\int_1^6y\,dx\approx$
questions.corrige_markdown:
The six ordinates $y_1,\dots,y_6$ are equally spaced with $h=1$ (five strips). The trapezium rule gives
$\displaystyle\int_1^6y\,dx\approx\dfrac h2\left[y_1+y_6+2(y_2+y_3+y_4+y_5)\right]=\dfrac12\left[2+6.3+2(3.2+4.2+5+5.7)\right]$
$=\dfrac12\left[8.3+2(18.1)\right]=\dfrac12(44.5)=22.25$.

Traps: B, $26.40$, is just the sum of all ordinates; D, $34.70$, is first plus last plus the sum of all ordinates ($8.3+26.4$); C is a digit transposition of the correct value.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The number of arrangements of the letters of the word SUCCEEDED is
questions.corrige_markdown:
SUCCEEDED has $9$ letters: S (1), U (1), C (2), E (3), D (2). When some letters are repeated, the number of distinct arrangements is $\dfrac{9!}{2!\,3!\,2!}$ (one factorial for each repeated letter: C twice, E three times, D twice). Numerically $\dfrac{362880}{24}=15120$.

Option A omits one of the two repeated pairs; options C and D start from $5!$ (the number of distinct letters), which is not the number of positions.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The equations of the vertical asymptotes to the graph of $f(x)=\dfrac{8}{x^2-4}$ are
questions.corrige_markdown:
Vertical asymptotes occur where the denominator is zero and the numerator is not: $x^2-4=(x-2)(x+2)=0$ gives $x=2$ and $x=-2$; the numerator $8$ is never zero, so $f(x)\to\pm\infty$ as $x\to\pm2$. The asymptotes are $x=-2$ and $x=2$. (There is also a horizontal asymptote $y=0$.)

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The solution set of the inequality $\dfrac{x+2}{x-1}\ge0$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The fraction changes sign only at $x=-2$ (numerator zero) and $x=1$ (denominator zero, undefined).

| Interval | $x+2$ | $x-1$ | Fraction |
|---|---|---|---|
| $x<-2$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ |
| $-2<x<1$ | $+$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $x>1$ | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ |

The fraction is non-negative for $x<-2$ and $x>1$; at $x=-2$ it equals $0$ so $x=-2$ is included, and at $x=1$ it is undefined so $x=1$ is excluded. Solution set: $x\le-2$ or $x>1$. Option C wrongly includes $x=1$.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A committee of $5$, with at least one boy and one girl, is to be formed from $3$ boys and $5$ girls. The number of ways this committee can be form if there are to be more girls than boys is
questions.corrige_markdown:
A committee of $5$ with more girls than boys has at least $3$ girls. Since it must contain at least one boy, the possible compositions (boys, girls) are $(1,4)$ and $(2,3)$; $(0,5)$ is excluded because there must be a boy.

- $1$ boy and $4$ girls: $\binom31\binom54=3\times5=15$.
- $2$ boys and $3$ girls: $\binom32\binom53=3\times10=30$.

Total $=15+30=45$. Options B and C are only one of the two cases.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The value of $a$ for which the quadratic equation $ax^2-10x+4=0$ has equal roots is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Equal roots require the discriminant to be zero: $b^2-4ac=(-10)^2-4a(4)=100-16a=0$, so $a=\dfrac{100}{16}=\dfrac{25}{4}$ (and $a\neq0$, so the equation is quadratic). Then the double root is $x=\dfrac{10}{2a}=\dfrac45$.

Option B, $\dfrac4{25}$, is the reciprocal; A and C have a wrong sign.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A linear reduction of a relationship $y=ax^{n-1}$, produced the result $\log y=4\log x+2$. The values of the constants $\log a$ and $n$ are
questions.corrige_markdown:
Take logarithms of $y=ax^{n-1}$: $\log y=(n-1)\log x+\log a$. This is a straight line in the variables $\log x$ (horizontal) and $\log y$ (vertical) with gradient $n-1$ and intercept $\log a$.

Compare with $\log y=4\log x+2$: $n-1=4$, so $n=5$, and $\log a=2$ (so $a=100$ with common logarithms). Option C takes $n=3$ ($n-1=2$ confused with the intercept).

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The cardinality of set of $X=\{a,b,c\}$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The cardinality $n(X)$ of a finite set is its number of elements. $X=\{a,b,c\}$ has three elements, so $n(X)=3$.

Option B, $8=2^3$, is the number of subsets of $X$ (the cardinality of the power set), a different quantity.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The Cartesian equation of the curve with parametric equations $x=1-t^2$ and $y=4t$, where $t$ is a parameter is
questions.corrige_markdown:
From $y=4t$: $t=\dfrac y4$. Substitute into $x=1-t^2$: $x=1-\dfrac{y^2}{16}$, so $16x=16-y^2$.

Check: $16(1-t^2)=16-16t^2=16-(4t)^2=16-y^2$. Option B would correspond to $y=2t$; options A and D have the wrong sign.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION B: MECHANICS**

The position vector of a particle of mass $3$ kg is $\mathbf r=\left[t^2\mathbf i-2t\mathbf j+(1-t^3)\mathbf k\right]$ m. Its momentum when $t=1$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Velocity $\mathbf v=\dfrac{d\mathbf r}{dt}=2t\,\mathbf i-2\,\mathbf j-3t^2\,\mathbf k$ (m s$^{-1}$); at $t=1$: $\mathbf v=2\mathbf i-2\mathbf j-3\mathbf k$.

Momentum $\mathbf p=m\mathbf v=3(2\mathbf i-2\mathbf j-3\mathbf k)=(6\mathbf i-6\mathbf j-9\mathbf k)\ \mathrm{N\,s}$.

Option B is the velocity (the mass has been forgotten).

**Answer: D.**

themes: motion of a vehicle with resistance
questions.enonce_markdown: A truck of mass $1800$ kg is moving along a straight level road against a constant resistance of $800$ N. Given that the engine of the car is working at $40$ kW when the speed of the car is $20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, the acceleration of the car is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Take the direction of motion as positive. The power is $P=Fv$, so the driving force is $F=\dfrac Pv=\dfrac{40\,000\ \mathrm W}{20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}}=2000\ \mathrm N$.

The road is level, so the only horizontal forces are the driving force $F$ forwards and the resistance $R=800$ N backwards. Newton's second law: $F-R=ma$, so $2000-800=1800\,a$ and $a=\dfrac{1200}{1800}=\dfrac23\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

Options A, B and D do not come from this balance (for instance $\frac{2000}{1800}\approx1.1$ ignores the resistance).

**Answer: C.**

themes: elastic strings and potential energy mechanics
questions.enonce_markdown: When an elastic string is stretched to a length of $1.8$ m, the tension in the string is $14$ N. Given that the modulus of elasticity of the string is $28$ N, the natural length of the string is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Hooke's law: $T=\dfrac{\lambda x}{l_0}$ with modulus $\lambda=28$ N, natural length $l_0$ and extension $x=1.8-l_0$:
$14=\dfrac{28(1.8-l_0)}{l_0}$, so $14\,l_0=28(1.8-l_0)$, $l_0=2(1.8-l_0)$, $3l_0=3.6$ and $l_0=1.2$ m.

Check: extension $0.6$ m, so $T=\dfrac{28\times0.6}{1.2}=14$ N. Option B, $0.6$ m, is the extension, not the natural length.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A particle is projected from a point on a horizontal plane with speed $V$ at an angle $\theta$ to the plane. The greatest height $H$ attained by the particle is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Vertical motion (upwards positive): initial vertical velocity $V\sin\theta$, acceleration $-g$. At the greatest height the vertical velocity is zero, so $0=(V\sin\theta)^2-2gH$, giving $H=\dfrac{V^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$.

Options C and D contain $\sin2\theta$: the expression $\dfrac{V^2\sin2\theta}{g}$ (D) is the horizontal range, not the height. Option A has the factor $2$ in the wrong place.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A particle of mass $3$ kg is moving in a horizontal circle of radius $1$ m. The centripetal force is $48$ N. The angular speed of the particle is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The centripetal force is $F=m\omega^2r$, so $48=3\,\omega^2(1)$, $\omega^2=16$ and $\omega=4\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ (positive root).

Option A, $16$, is $\omega^2$ (the square root was not taken).

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A smooth sphere $B$ of mass $6$ kg travelling with speed $3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ collides directly with another smooth sphere $A$ of mass $4$ kg travelling with the same speed as $B$ but in the opposite direction. Sphere $B$ is brought to rest by the impact. The kinetic energy of $A$ after impact is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Take the initial direction of $B$ as positive. Before the impact: $B$ has velocity $+3$ and $A$ has velocity $-3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Conservation of linear momentum along the line of centres (no external horizontal impulse):
$6(3)+4(-3)=6(0)+4v_A$, so $6=4v_A$ and $v_A=1.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ (in the original direction of $B$).

Kinetic energy of $A$ after impact: $\tfrac12(4)(1.5)^2=4.5\ \mathrm J=\dfrac92$ J.

Consistency: the speed of separation is $1.5$ and the speed of approach is $6$, so $e=0.25\in[0,1]$, and kinetic energy decreases from $45$ J to $4.5$ J, so the data are physically possible. Option D, $18$ J, is $\tfrac12(4)(3)^2$, the energy of $A$ before impact.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The work done by a force $(-2\mathbf i+5\mathbf j)$ N which moves a particle from a point $A$ to another point $B$, where $\overrightarrow{OA}=(-\mathbf i-3\mathbf j)$ m and $\overrightarrow{OB}=(2\mathbf i+\mathbf j)$ m, is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The displacement from $A$ to $B$ is $\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{OB}-\overrightarrow{OA}=(2\mathbf i+\mathbf j)-(-\mathbf i-3\mathbf j)=(3\mathbf i+4\mathbf j)$ m.

Work done by a constant force: $W=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf d=(-2)(3)+(5)(4)=-6+20=14$ J.

Traps: using $\overrightarrow{OB}$ alone gives $-4+5=1$ J (A); using $\overrightarrow{OA}$ alone gives $2-15=-13$ J (B is its opposite); D is the opposite of the correct value (displacement taken from $B$ to $A$).

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The magnitude of the resultant of the forces $\mathbf F_1=(-5\mathbf i+12\mathbf j)$ N, $\mathbf F_2=(-18\mathbf i-8\mathbf j)$ N, $\mathbf F_3=(4\mathbf i+9\mathbf j)$ N and $\mathbf F_4=(4\mathbf i-5\mathbf j)$ N is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Add the components: $\mathbf i$: $-5-18+4+4=-15$; $\mathbf j$: $12-8+9-5=8$. The resultant is $\mathbf R=(-15\mathbf i+8\mathbf j)$ N and
$|\mathbf R|=\sqrt{(-15)^2+8^2}=\sqrt{225+64}=\sqrt{289}=17$ N.

Options A ($15+8$) and C ($15-8$) add or subtract the components instead of using Pythagoras.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A girl on a ship, whose velocity is $(4\mathbf i-7\mathbf j)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ is watching a boat whose velocity is $(-8\mathbf i-2\mathbf j)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The speed of the boat as it appears to the girl is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The velocity of the boat relative to the girl is $\mathbf v_{B/G}=\mathbf v_B-\mathbf v_G=(-8\mathbf i-2\mathbf j)-(4\mathbf i-7\mathbf j)=(-12\mathbf i+5\mathbf j)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

The question asks for the speed, which is the magnitude (a scalar): $\sqrt{(-12)^2+5^2}=\sqrt{169}=13\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

Option A is the relative velocity (a vector, not a speed); B is the velocity of the girl relative to the boat; D comes from an arithmetic slip.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Two events $A$ and $B$ are such that $P(A|B)=\dfrac{11}{21}$ and $P(B)=\dfrac35$, then $P(A\cap B)=$
questions.corrige_markdown:
By definition $P(A|B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$, so $P(A\cap B)=P(A|B)\,P(B)=\dfrac{11}{21}\times\dfrac35=\dfrac{33}{105}=\dfrac{11}{35}$.

(Dividing instead of multiplying would give $\dfrac{55}{63}$, which is not an option.)

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The diagram shows two particles $P$ and $Q$ hanging freely and connected by a light inextensible string passing over a fixed smooth pulley. The system is released from rest. Taking $g$ as $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, the acceleration of $P$ and the tension in the string are

![fig-1](gce-al-pm-mechanics-2025-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
From the figure: the weight of $P$ is $10$ N and the weight of $Q$ is $40$ N. With $g=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ the masses are $m_P=1$ kg and $m_Q=4$ kg.

The string is light and inextensible and the pulley is smooth, so the tension $T$ is the same on both sides and both particles have accelerations of the same magnitude $a$. $Q$ is heavier, so $Q$ moves down and $P$ moves up.

Equation for $P$ (upwards positive): $T-10=1\cdot a$.
Equation for $Q$ (downwards positive): $40-T=4a$.

Adding: $30=5a$, so $a=6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Then $T=10+6=16$ N. Check with $Q$: $40-16=24=4\times6$.

Options B and C have $a=10$ (free fall), which would need $T=0$.

**Answer: D.**

themes: centre of mass of composite bodies
questions.enonce_markdown: Three particles of weight $7$ N, $9$ N and $4$ N have position vector $(4\mathbf i+\mathbf j)$ m, $3\mathbf j$ m and $(3\mathbf i+4\mathbf j)$ m respectively. The position vector of their centre of mass is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The weights are proportional to the masses (the same $g$), so the centre of mass is $\bar{\mathbf r}=\dfrac{\sum w_i\mathbf r_i}{\sum w_i}$ with $\sum w_i=7+9+4=20$ N.

$\sum w_i\mathbf r_i=7(4\mathbf i+\mathbf j)+9(3\mathbf j)+4(3\mathbf i+4\mathbf j)=(28+12)\mathbf i+(7+27+16)\mathbf j=40\mathbf i+50\mathbf j$.

$\bar{\mathbf r}=\dfrac{40\mathbf i+50\mathbf j}{20}=\left(2\mathbf i+\dfrac52\mathbf j\right)$ m.

Option C is the unnormalised sum of moments (not divided by $20$); option A is the unweighted mean of the positions, $\dfrac{(4+0+3)\mathbf i+(1+3+4)\mathbf j}{3}$.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The speed of a particle at time $t$ seconds is given by $v=(3t^2+6t+2)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The distance travelled by the particle between $t=1$ s and $t=4$ s is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The speed is positive for $t>0$, so the particle never reverses and the distance equals the integral of the speed:
$s=\displaystyle\int_1^4(3t^2+6t+2)\,dt=\left[t^3+3t^2+2t\right]_1^4=(64+48+8)-(1+3+2)=120-6=114$ m.

Option D is $120+6$ (sign slip when subtracting the lower limit).

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A car moving at $5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ is brought to rest after travelling a distance of $1.5$ km. The acceleration of the car is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Take the direction of motion as positive: $u=5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $v=0$, $s=1.5\ \mathrm{km}=1500$ m. From $v^2=u^2+2as$: $0=25+2a(1500)$, so $a=-\dfrac{25}{3000}=-\dfrac1{120}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ (a deceleration).

Options A and B use $s=1.5$ m (the distance was not converted from km to m). Option C has the wrong sign: the car slows down, so the acceleration is negative.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Two fair dice are thrown on a floor, the probability that the same scores are obtained is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The sample space has $6\times6=36$ equally likely outcomes. The outcomes with the same score on both dice are $(1,1),(2,2),\dots,(6,6)$: $6$ outcomes. So $P=\dfrac6{36}=\dfrac16$.

Option B, $\dfrac1{36}$, is the probability of one particular double (for example two sixes); option A, $\dfrac56$, is the probability of different scores.

**Answer: D.**
